# Appendix III: 2026 IOTC Technical Workshops and Meetings {#workshops}

## Capacity building workshops

To support further progress in the implementation of the IOTC Regional Observer Scheme (ROS), the Secretariat organised three capacity-building workshops in 2026, focusing on data collection and reporting requirements for different fishing gear groups. These workshops aimed to strengthen CPCs' understanding of ROS reporting requirements, promote the use of standardised reporting forms and improve the quality and completeness of observer data submitted to the IOTC.

### Technical workshop to improve the reporting of purse seine data to the IOTC

The Workshop on Purse Seine Fisheries Reporting was held in Seychelles, a country that has hosted one of the largest purse seine fisheries in the Indian Ocean for several decades. Conducted from 16 to 19 March, the workshop brought together 18 participants from six CPCs with industrial purse seine fleets operating in the Indian Ocean. Participants included representatives from fishing industries responsible for purse seine vessels, as well as companies involved in the development of software for the collection and processing of purse seine fisheries data, including Regional Observer Scheme (ROS) data.

Given the workshop's focus on purse seine fisheries reporting, discussions and technical reviews addressed all mandatory reporting requirements for the fishery, including retained catch, catch and effort, size-frequency data, information on fishing activities associated with drifting Floating Objects (dFOBs), buoy usage, and the implementation and evaluation of Regional Observer Scheme (ROS) data collection programmes by CPCs. Several presentations provided an overview of the current status of these datasets, highlighting both achievements and challenges in data collection and reporting. Particular attention was given to the development of data validation tools and the ongoing review of the dFAD reporting form. Participants were also introduced to the revised ROS reporting format and accompanying guidelines, including reporting requirements and implementation considerations.
A presentation on the ObServe software by the Institut de Recherche pour le Developpement (IRD) highlighted the importance of collecting high-quality fisheries and scientific observer data from purse seine vessels. The software was well received, particularly by CPCs that are still developing their fisheries data management systems for purse seine fleets. Currently, the software is being used by the European purse seine fleet and Seychelles. In response to the strong interest expressed by participants, IRD proposed organizing a dedicated training workshop on the use of ObServe. The Secretariat also committed to ensuring that all reference codes incorporated into the software remain current and aligned with IOTC reporting standards.
The workshop also discussed how Electronic Monitoring (EM) data could be integrated into the existing ROS framework to enhance monitoring coverage and improve the quality and completeness of data collected from purse seine fisheries.

### ROS reporting workshop for longline fisheries

The ROS Reporting Workshop for Longline Fisheries was held in Johannesburg from 26 to 29 May 2026 and brought together 12 participants from eight CPCs. The workshop also benefited from the participation of experts in fisheries observer programmes and electronic monitoring, who shared their knowledge and experiences with participants.

The workshop focused on the implementation and reporting requirements of the Regional Observer Scheme (ROS) for longline fisheries. CPC representatives presented the status of their national ROS programmes, including data collection and reporting workflows, as well as the challenges encountered in programme implementation and data submission. The Secretariat provided an overview of the evolution of the ROS, identified key data gaps, and presented recent developments in reporting forms, reporting requirements, and associated guidelines.
Given the increasing use of Electronic Monitoring (EM) systems in longline fisheries for the collection of observer-related data, the workshop also reviewed existing data gaps and discussed the implications of EM-derived data for ROS reporting requirements and data management processes.

Unlike purse seine fisheries, where dedicated software solutions are available to support the collection and management of observer and fisheries data, no common software platform is currently used for ROS data collection in longline fisheries. Instead, individual fleets and CPCs have developed their own tools and procedures for collecting, managing, and reporting ROS data. This diversity of approaches highlighted the importance of harmonising data standards and reporting practices to improve data quality, consistency, and reporting efficiency across CPCs.

### Gillnet data collection under the IOTC ROS

The Workshop on Gillnet Fisheries Data Collection was conducted remotely and brought together representatives from CPCs with significant gillnet fisheries, namely Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Iran, and Pakistan. Over two days, comprising a total of six hours of discussions, participants reviewed the importance of gillnet fisheries in the Indian Ocean and recent developments in the fishery. Given that gillnet fisheries are predominantly small- to medium-scale operations, participants acknowledged the considerable challenges associated with data collection, resulting in limited and often fragmented data available for assessment and management purposes.
Building on discussions from previous workshops related to the Regional Observer Scheme (ROS), participants reiterated the long-standing challenges of implementing conventional observer programmes aboard gillnet vessels. These challenges remain largely unchanged and include the small size of vessels, onboard safety concerns, limited accommodation, and generally unsuitable conditions for non-fishers to remain at sea for extended periods.

The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF)-Pakistan initiated a crew-based observer programme in Pakistan in 2012, covering a number of gillnet vessels and generating a substantial amount of fisheries data. During the workshop, two presentations were delivered on the programme. The first provided an overview of its development and implementation, while the second focused on the design of the associated data collection system. WWF-Pakistan worked closely with the Secretariat to develop data collection forms aligned with IOTC reporting requirements. Although the programme generated valuable information, it was discontinued in 2019. Furthermore, as WWF acted as a secondary data holder rather than the competent authority, the data collected through the programme were not formally submitted to the Secretariat.
A crew-based observer programme has been operating on a trial basis in Sri Lanka since 2018. Given the scale and diversity of the country's gillnet fisheries, including vessels operating both within areas under national jurisdiction and on the high seas, different management and monitoring arrangements apply across fisheries. As a result, the implementation of the crew-based observer programme has progressed at varying rates, reflecting the differing operational and management contexts.

For high-seas gillnet fisheries, the crew-based observer programme follows a data collection format closely aligned with the Regional Observer Scheme (ROS), covering most of the required data fields. While some information is not currently collected, this is largely due to the absence of specific fields in the existing data collection forms rather than operational constraints, and could be readily incorporated if required. The programme is primarily funded by the private fishing sector and is implemented through close collaboration between industry stakeholders and the Sri Lankan Government.

In contrast, Iran and Indonesia currently do not operate observer programmes within their gillnet fisheries. Data collection in these fisheries relies primarily on port sampling and landing-site monitoring.

In Iran, port sampling is largely limited to tuna and tuna-like species. Biological information for non-target species is generally unavailable, as many fish are processed at sea or prior to landing, resulting in catches being landed in a headed and gutted condition. Iran expressed interest in exploring a crew-based observer approach, recognising its potential to improve biological data collection while remaining cost-effective and fostering greater collaboration with fishers.

Indonesia, meanwhile, presented its recently introduced OBOR application, which has been in use since 2025 and employs artificial intelligence (AI) to support species identification and catch enumeration. The system was developed to strengthen fisheries data collection and processing; however, it remains unclear to what extent it has been implemented within gillnet fisheries, given that Indonesia does not have a gillnet fleet operating beyond areas under national jurisdiction.

The workshop concluded with a proposal to organise an in-person meeting focused on alternative data collection approaches for gillnet fisheries, including practical training on data requirements and collection methodologies. Participants also requested an independent review of existing ROS data collection approaches, including conventional observer programmes, crew-based observation systems, and emerging electronic monitoring and technology-based solutions, with the aim of identifying best practices and improving data coverage across gillnet fisheries in the Indian Ocean.

## Participation in Other Workshops

The Data Section participated in three other workshops in 2026 related to fisheries data management.

The International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) workshop aimed to improve understanding of the impacts of large-scale and small-scale tropical tuna fisheries, with particular emphasis on data and governance gaps. Representatives from several tuna Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (t-RFMOs) participated and presented the current status of tropical tuna fisheries within their respective management areas. Discussions highlighted differences in data availability, reporting obligations, and management approaches between fisheries and regions. A key recommendation from the workshop was the need for greater collaboration among t-RFMOs to review and harmonise data requirements, while improving alignment between reporting obligations and management measures. During the workshop, the Data Coordinator presented a case study on large-scale and small-scale fisheries within the IOTC area of competence. The presentation highlighted the absence of a universally accepted definition and classification of artisanal, small-scale, and subsistence fisheries across CPCs, and the challenges this creates for data collection, and reporting. The ongoing efforts by the Secretariat to improve the categorisation of these fisheries and to support more consistent reporting practices across CPCs were also presented and discussed.

The Indian Ocean Shark Research Plan workshop focused on identifying research priorities and data requirements to support the development of a coordinated regional research plan for sharks. Discussions included a review of existing IOTC shark data holdings, their availability and reporting status, and the main gaps and challenges affecting the collection, reporting and use of shark fisheries data. The workshop provided an opportunity to identify priority research needs and opportunities to improve data collection and availability in support of shark stock assessments and management.

The Data Section participated in a technical webinar organised by FAO and the Southeast Asian Fisheries Development Center (SEAFDEC) on 14 October 2026. The webinar reviewed existing approaches and frameworks for collecting and reporting information on abandoned, lost or otherwise discarded fishing gear (ALDFG). Discussions highlighted opportunities to harmonise data collection methods, reporting procedures and terminology, with a view to improving the consistency and comparability of ALDFG information and supporting the development of regional guidelines.

## External meetings

The Data Section participated in four external meetings held virtually in 2026. Two of the meetings were related to European Union fisheries data status, while the other two focused on bycatch-related data.
